claim: Emiliania huxleyi is a model coccolithophore micro-alga that generates vast blooms in the ocean.
source: Emiliania huxleyi is a model coccolithophore micro-alga that generates vast blooms in the ocean.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about E. huxleyi as a well-studied organism.

claim: Phaeobacter inhibens is a well-studied member of the Roseobacter group.
source: the bacterium Phaeobacter inhibens, a well-studied member of the Roseobacter group
evidence: This is established knowledge about the taxonomic classification of P. inhibens.

claim: While attached to the algal cell, bacteria initially promote algal growth but ultimately kill their algal host.
source: While attached to the algal cell, bacteria initially promote algal growth but ultimately kill their algal host.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4a and Figure 6.

claim: Both algal growth enhancement and algal death are driven by the bacterially-produced phytohormone indole-3-acetic acid.
source: Both algal growth enhancement and algal death are driven by the bacterially-produced phytohormone indole-3-acetic acid.
evidence: This is supported by data showing IAA production by bacteria (Figure 4b) and its effects on algal growth at different concentrations (Figure 4c).

claim: Bacterial production of indole-3-acetic acid and attachment to algae are significantly increased by tryptophan, which is exuded from the algal cell.
source: Bacterial production of indole-3-acetic acid and attachment to algae are significantly increased by tryptophan, which is exuded from the algal cell.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased IAA production with tryptophan addition (Figure 5a) and detection of tryptophan in algal supernatant (Figure 5c).

claim: Algal death triggered by bacteria involves activation of pathways unique to oxidative stress response and programmed cell death.
source: Algal death triggered by bacteria involves activation of pathways unique to oxidative stress response and programmed cell death.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data (Table 1) and TUNEL assay results (Figure 6q-t).

claim: Coccolithophores are fundamental in the global oxygen, carbon, and sulfur cycles due to their high abundance.
source: Because of their high abundance, these micro-algae are fundamental in the global oxygen, carbon, and sulfur cycles (Balch et al., 1991; Beaufort et al., 2011; Simó, 2001; Field et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Coccolithophores, together with other phytoplankton, are responsible for nearly half of the planet's primary production.
source: As a consequence of their photosynthetic capacity these algae, together with other phytoplankton, are responsible for nearly half of our planet's primary production (Field et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Field et al., 1998.

claim: Coccolith production by E. huxleyi accounts for roughly 1/3 of the total marine calcium carbonate production.
source: Coccolith production by E. huxleyi accounts for roughly 1/3 of the total marine calcium carbonate production (Iglesias-Rodríguez et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Iglesias-Rodríguez et al., 2002.

claim: Emiliania huxleyi is the most widespread coccolithophore in modern oceans, forming dense annual blooms.
source: Emiliania huxleyi is the most widespread coccolithophore in modern oceans, forming dense annual blooms (Paasche, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Paasche, 2001.

claim: E. huxleyi blooms can cover thousands of square kilometers of ocean surfaces and are easily detected by satellites due to the highly reflective nature of the coccoliths.
source: The blooms can cover thousands of square kilometers of ocean surfaces and are easily detected by satellites due to the highly reflective nature of the coccoliths (Balch et al., 1991; Holligan et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Balch et al., 1991 and Holligan et al., 1983.

claim: E. huxleyi blooms form seasonally over several weeks and then suddenly collapse.
source: The blooms also exhibit unique dynamics; they form seasonally over several weeks and then suddenly collapse (Behrenfeld and Boss, 2014; Lehahn et al., 2014; Tyrrell and Merico, 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Bloom collapse has been attributed to viral infection.
source: they form seasonally over several weeks and then suddenly collapse (Behrenfeld and Boss, 2014; Lehahn et al., 2014; Tyrrell and Merico, 2004), a process that has been attributed to viral infection (Bratbak et al., 1993; Lehahn et al., 2014; Vardi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bratbak et al., 1993; Lehahn et al., 2014; Vardi et al., 2012.

claim: Environmental stresses and viral infection can trigger oxidative stress and a process similar to programmed cell death (PCD) in E. huxleyi.
source: Recent evidence suggests that environmental stresses and viral infection can trigger oxidative stress and a process similar to programmed cell death (PCD) in E. huxleyi (Bidle et al., 2007; Vardi et al., 2009; Bidle, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bidle et al., 2007; Vardi et al., 2009; Bidle, 2016.

claim: E. huxleyi blooms harbor a rich community of bacteria, at times dominated by the Roseobacter group.
source: Interestingly, although E. huxleyi blooms harbor a rich community of bacteria, at times dominated by the Roseobacter group (González et al., 2000; Green et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to González et al., 2000; Green et al., 2015.

claim: Bacteria are not generally considered to be a factor influencing coccolithophore physiology and bloom dynamics.
source: bacteria are not generally considered to be a factor influencing coccolithophore physiology and bloom dynamics.
evidence: This represents the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: P. inhibens was found co-occurring with E. huxleyi in algal blooms in the Gulf of Maine.
source: The results shown in Figure 1 indicate that P. inhibens was indeed found co-occurring with E. huxleyi in algal blooms (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis data shown in Figure 1.

claim: P. inhibens does not grow alone in L1-Si medium.
source: Of note, alone these bacteria do not grow in the L1-Si medium (Figure 2d, grey bars).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Bacteria grow in co-culture with E. huxleyi in L1-Si medium.
source: However, we found that bacteria do grow in co-culture with E. huxleyi.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: In co-cultures, bacterial numbers increased nearly five orders of magnitude over a period of 14 days.
source: In these co-cultures, bacterial numbers increased nearly five orders of magnitude over a period of 14 days (Figure 2d, green bars).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: In co-cultures, some algae were no longer surrounded by coccoliths and naked algal cells were covered by bacteria attached via their poles.
source: Microscopic examination of the co-culture revealed that some algae were no longer surrounded by coccoliths (Figure 2e). Rather, naked algal cells were now covered by bacteria attached via their poles.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy images in Figure 2e and 2f.

claim: Bacterial attachment onto the algal cell involves the polar bacterial polysaccharide.
source: Using a specific fluorescent lectin to detect the polar polysaccharide (see Materials and methods), it appeared that bacterial attachment onto the algal cell also involves the polar bacterial polysaccharide (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescent lectin staining shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Over time more algae have attached bacteria in co-cultures.
source: Examination of co-cultures revealed that over time more algae have attached bacteria (Figure 2g)
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Each algal cell is associated with increasing numbers of bacteria as the co-culture ages.
source: each algal cell is associated with increasing numbers of bacteria as the co-culture ages (Figure 2f,h).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Addition of 5.5 mM glucose to L1-Si did not lead to significant bacterial growth.
source: However, addition of 5.5 mM glucose did not lead to significant bacterial growth (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Addition of higher nutrient concentrations as individual supplements or in various combinations of two or three did not lead to robust bacterial growth.
source: In fact, even addition of higher nutrient concentrations in forms shown to be utilizable by P. inhibens (Zech et al., 2009) as individual supplements (nitrogen 5 mM NH4, phosphorous 2 mM PO4, and sulfur 33 mM SO4) or in various combinations of two or three of them did not lead to robust bacterial growth (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Addition of all four essential nutrients (C, N, P, S) resulted in bacterial growth to a density of 5×10^8 CFU/ml.
source: Only addition of all four essential nutrients resulted in bacterial growth to a density of 5×108 CFU/ml, which we normalized to 100% in Figure 3a.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: E. huxleyi can provide all four essential nutrients (C, N, P and S) in suitable forms and concentrations to enable growth of P. inhibens.
source: Thus, E. huxleyi can provide all four essential nutrients (C, N, P and S) in suitable forms and concentrations to enable growth of the heterotrophic bacterium P. inhibens.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing bacterial growth in co-culture but not with individual nutrients.

claim: DMSP can serve as a sulfur source for P. inhibens.
source: As shown in Figure 3a, DMSP can serve as a sulfur source (Figure 3a, 'CNP + DMSP 30 μM').
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: DMSP does not supply sufficient carbon to support robust bacterial growth.
source: In contrast, DMSP does not supply sufficient carbon to support robust bacterial growth. (Figure 3a 'NP + DMSP 30 μM').
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: All of the added DMSP is rapidly utilized by growing bacteria.
source: Our measurements indicate that all of the added DMSP is rapidly utilized by the growing bacteria whereas in un-inoculated medium the DMSP levels remain relatively stable over time (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Over a period of 17 days, DMSP concentration in the medium of a pure algal culture increased, reaching a concentration of nearly 6 µM.
source: Indeed, over a period of 17 days, DMSP concentration in the medium of a pure algal culture increased, reaching a concentration of nearly 6 µM (Figure 3c, black bars).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: In a co-culture of algae and bacteria, DMSP levels in the medium were nearly undetectable.
source: In contrast, in a co-culture of algae and bacteria, DMSP levels in the medium were nearly undetectable, presumably due to its rapid metabolism by the bacteria (Figure 3c, grey bars).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: During the initial 10 days of culturing, there were greater numbers of algae in the co-cultures compared to pure algal cultures.
source: We found that during the initial 10 days of culturing, there were greater numbers of algae in the co-cultures compared to pure algal cultures (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: In the co-culture, algae reach approximately 25% higher numbers in comparison with the maximum reached in the absence of bacteria.
source: In the co-culture, algae reach approximately 25% higher numbers in comparison with the maximum reached in the absence of bacteria.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: In an algal pure culture the death phase starts after day seven while in a co-culture a significant decrease in population is evident only at day 17.
source: In addition, in an algal pure culture the death phase starts after day seven while in a co-culture a significant decrease in population is evident only at day 17.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The death phase in an algal pure culture seems more gradual than the rapid demise observed in a co-culture.
source: Interestingly, the death phase in an algal pure culture seems more gradual than the rapid demise observed in a co-culture (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: IAA (0.4 nM) was detected in P. inhibens pure cultures.
source: We were able to detect IAA (0.4 nM) in bacterial pure cultures (see Materials and methods) (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: No IAA was detected in axenic algal cultures.
source: Importantly, no IAA was detected in axenic algal cultures.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Algal growth yield was improved by 20% upon addition of 1 µM and 100 µM IAA.
source: Similar to the increase we observed in co-culture, algal growth yield was improved by 20% upon addition of 1 µM and 100 µM IAA (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: IAA was undetectable in co-cultures, suggesting rapid up-take by algae.
source: Our attempts to monitor IAA levels in co-cultures revealed that in these conditions IAA was undetectable, suggesting rapid up-take by algae.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inability to detect IAA in co-cultures.

claim: Addition of 0.1 mM tryptophan resulted in the production of 10.8 nM IAA, approximately 25-fold increase in comparison to conditions with no added tryptophan.
source: Indeed, addition of 0.1 mM tryptophan resulted in the production of 10.8 nM IAA, approximately 25-fold increase in comparison to conditions with no added tryptophan (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: All produced IAA from labeled tryptophan is fully labeled, indicating that exogenous tryptophan is directly converted to IAA.
source: The results of our experiments indicate that all produced IAA is fully labeled (Figure 5b), thus indicating that exogenous tryptophan is directly converted to IAA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by isotope labeling experiments shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Cultivation of a tryptophan auxotroph E. coli strain in minimal medium supplemented with filtered algal supernatant resulted in marked bacterial growth.
source: Cultivation of this strain in minimal medium supplemented with filtered algal supernatant resulted in marked bacterial growth (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Algal exudates contain bioavailable tryptophan.
source: This indicates that algal exudates contain bioavailable tryptophan.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth of tryptophan auxotroph in algal supernatant.

claim: Tryptophan (100 nM) was detected in filtered samples of E. huxleyi blooms.
source: Interestingly, we detected tryptophan (100 nM) in filtered samples of E. huxleyi blooms (see Materials and methods)
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation from environmental samples.

claim: After 17 days of incubation the color of the co-cultures rapidly changed from green to white, a process referred to as 'bleaching'.
source: However, after 17 days of incubation the color of the co-cultures rapidly changed from green (the color of healthy algae) to white, a process we refer to as 'bleaching' (Figure 6c,d and Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by images shown in Figure 6c,d and Video 1.

claim: Algal cells in a bleached co-culture exhibit more coccolith shedding.
source: This revealed that the algal cells in a bleached co-culture exhibit more coccolith shedding (Figure 6e,f,g,h, note arrow in Figure 6h).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy images shown in Figure 6e-h.

claim: The typical fluorescent crescent shape made of the two chloroplasts in each cell is lost in the bleached co-culture and the fluorescent signal fills the entire cell.
source: Furthermore, the typical fluorescent crescent shape that is made of the two chloroplasts in each cell (Figure 6i,j,k) is lost in the bleached co-culture and the fluorescent signal emanating from chlorophyll and accessory pigments fills the entire cell (Figure 6l).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 6i-l.

claim: The aging co-culture contains mostly dead algal cells as indicated by viability staining.
source: In addition, using a viability stain (Sytox green, see Materials and methods) it is evident that the aging co-culture contains mostly dead algal cells (Figure 6m,n,o,p).
evidence: This is demonstrated by viability staining shown in Figure 6m-p.

claim: At day 17, the vast majority of algal cells in the co-culture are dead (94%) while in the pure culture only 21% are dead.
source: At this time point, the vast majority of algal cells in the co-culture are dead (94% as indicated by Sytox staining, see Figure 3p) while in the pure culture only 21% are dead by day 17.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of viability staining shown in Figure 6p.

claim: 15 genes encoding proteins involved in oxidative stress and programmed cell death exhibited significant up-regulation in algae over time in co-culture.
source: Out of 50 examined genes representing various functional groups (Supplementary file 1), 15 genes exhibited significant up-regulation in algae over time in co-culture (Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by gene expression data shown in Table 1.

claim: 90% of algal cells in 20-day old co-cultures contain highly fragmented DNA in comparison to 35% in axenic algal cultures of the same age.
source: Using the TUNEL assay (see Materials and methods) we could detect that 90% of algal cells in 20-day old co-cultures contain highly fragmented DNA in comparison to 35% in axenic algal cultures of the same age (Figure 6q–t).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 6q-t.

claim: Roseobacticides from P. inhibens kill the non-calcifying algal strain CCMP372 but do not kill the calcifying algal strain CCMP3266.
source: However, our results indicate that while roseobacticides from P. inhibens indeed kill the non-calcifying algal strain CCMP372 used in the previous study, they do not kill the calcifying algal strain CCMP3266 used in the current study (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: There is no detectable production of roseobacticides in co-culture conditions.
source: Moreover, there is no detectable production of roseobacticides in our co-culture conditions (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by HPLC analysis shown in Figure 7b.

claim: At concentrations between 1 and 100 µM IAA had a positive effect on algal growth, however 1000 µM proved to be harmful to algae.
source: At concentrations between 1 and 100 µM IAA had a positive effect on algal growth, however 1000 µM proved to be harmful to algae (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: P. inhibens mutants carrying mutations in various pathways of IAA synthesis were still capable of producing IAA.
source: In agreement with previous reports, these mutants were still capable of producing IAA (Table 2) (Spaepen et al., 2007)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Table 2 and supported by citation.

claim: A mutant in tryptophan biosynthesis (transposon mutant 1630) was unable to grow in pure culture without addition of tryptophan but exhibited robust growth in co-culture with algae.
source: Of note, a mutant in tryptophan biosynthesis (Table 2, transposon mutant 1630) was unable to grow in pure culture without addition of tryptophan (data not shown) but exhibited robust growth in co-culture with algae (Figure 8b)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 8b.

claim: A co-culture supplemented with 0.1 mM tryptophan undergoes accelerated death with bleaching occurring one week earlier than in non-treated co-cultures.
source: Our results indicate, that a co-culture that has been supplemented with 0.1 mM tryptophan undergoes accelerated death with bleaching occurring one week earlier than in non-treated co-cultures (Figure 9a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 9a.

claim: In cultures supplemented with tryptophan, bacteria became hyper-colonizers and attached to algal cells in significantly higher rates.
source: Moreover, examination under the microscope of co-cultures that have been treated with tryptophan revealed a remarkable change in bacterial behavior. In cultures supplemented with tryptophan, bacteria became hyper-colonizers and attached to algal cells in significantly higher rates (Figure 9b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy images shown in Figure 9b,c.

claim: Chlorophyll a measurements revealed similar concentrations in algal cells over a period of 17 days, whether in the presence or absence of bacteria.
source: However, chlorophyll a measurements revealed similar concentrations in algal cells over a period of 17 days, whether in the presence or absence of bacteria (Table 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by chlorophyll a measurements shown in Table 3.

claim: After bleaching, when the majority of the algal population was dead, a marked decrease in chlorophyll a concentration was evident.
source: Only after bleaching, when the majority of the algal population was dead, a marked decrease in chlorophyll a concentration was evident in agreement with the macroscopic phenotype of bleaching (Figure 6d) and microscopic phenotype of chloroplast deformation (Figure 6l) that are seen in the co-culture at the same time.
evidence: This is demonstrated by chlorophyll a measurements in Table 3 and images in Figure 6d and 6l.

claim: Bacteria in co-cultures were found attached solely to naked algal cells.
source: Bacteria in our co-cultures were found attached solely to naked algal cells.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from microscopy.

claim: Bacteria were not detected attached to calcified algae or shed coccoliths.
source: We did not detect bacteria attached to calcified algae or shed coccoliths.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from microscopy.

claim: Coccolithophores play a complex role in the global carbon cycle.
source: Hence, coccolithophores play a complex role in the global carbon cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the discussion of coccolith production and carbon dioxide release.

claim: During coccolith production, carbon dioxide is released and can escape from the ocean to the atmosphere.
source: During coccolith production, carbon dioxide is released and can escape from the ocean to the atmosphere (Marsh, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marsh, 2003.

claim: Coccoliths serve as a carbon sink as they accumulate on the bottom of the oceans.
source: More importantly, coccoliths serve as a carbon sink as they accumulate on the bottom of the oceans (Sabine et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sabine et al., 2004.

claim: E. huxleyi produces the osmolyte and antioxidant dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP).
source: E. huxleyi produces the osmolyte and antioxidant dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP) (Sunda et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sunda et al., 2002.

claim: DMSP, when released into the water by leakage or cell lysis, can be used by some bacteria as a source of sulfur and carbon.
source: This molecule, when released into the water by leakage or cell lysis, can be used by some bacteria as a source of sulfur and carbon (Curson et al., 2011; González et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Curson et al., 2011; González et al., 1999.

claim: During DMSP catabolism, bacteria such as Roseobacters produce the volatile by-product dimethyl sulfide (DMS).
source: During DMSP catabolism, bacteria such as Roseobacters produce the volatile by-product dimethyl sulfide (DMS).
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial DMSP metabolism.

claim: E. huxleyi is also a producer of DMS.
source: E. huxleyi is also a producer of DMS
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. huxleyi metabolism.

claim: When DMS enters the atmosphere it is oxidized and serves to form cloud condensation nuclei.
source: When DMS enters the atmosphere it is oxidized and serves to form cloud condensation nuclei (Curson et al., 2011; González et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Curson et al., 2011; González et al., 1999.

claim: The role of DMS in climate regulation has been questioned.
source: While the DMSP flux from algae to bacteria, and the production of DMS gas by both algae and bacteria have been clearly demonstrated, the role of DMS in climate regulation has been questioned (Quinn and Bates, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Quinn and Bates, 2011.

claim: P. inhibens, when grown in a pure culture in the presence of p-coumaric acid, produced novel compounds able to lyse E. huxleyi.
source: This bacterium, when grown in a pure culture in the presence of p-coumaric acid, a product released by aging algae, produced novel compounds able to lyse E. huxleyi.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to previous work by Seyedsayamdost et al., 2011.

claim: The compounds produced by P. inhibens that lyse E. huxleyi were named roseobacticides.
source: The compounds were named roseobacticides and their discovery pointed towards a possible interaction between P. inhibens and E. huxleyi (Seyedsayamdost et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Seyedsayamdost et al., 2011.

claim: Lipid metabolism in E. huxleyi is altered in the presence of P. inhibens.
source: Furthermore, we recently showed that lipid metabolism in E. huxleyi is altered in the presence of P. inhibens (Segev et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Segev et al., 2016.

claim: Various types of phytoplankton were shown to have both mutualistic and antagonistic interactions with bacteria.
source: Various types of phytoplankton were shown to have both mutualistic and antagonistic interactions with bacteria (Amin et al., 2015; Miller and Belas, 2004; Miller et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2014; Durham et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The possible role of algicidal bacteria in the ocean has been examined and discussed.
source: In addition, the possible role of algicidal bacteria in the ocean has been examined and discussed (Mayali and Azam, 2004; Harvey et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mayali and Azam, 2004; Harvey et al., 2016.

claim: IAA was previously demonstrated to play significant roles in numerous terrestrial plant-bacteria interactions.
source: Intriguingly, the auxin indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) was previously demonstrated to play significant roles in numerous terrestrial plant-bacteria interactions and was recently shown to be key in a marine association between a diatom and a Roseobacter bacterium (Amin et al., 2015; Spaepen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Amin et al., 2015; Spaepen et al., 2007.

claim: IAA was recently shown to be key in a marine association between a diatom and a Roseobacter bacterium.
source: the auxin indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) was previously demonstrated to play significant roles in numerous terrestrial plant-bacteria interactions and was recently shown to be key in a marine association between a diatom and a Roseobacter bacterium (Amin et al., 2015; Spaepen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Amin et al., 2015; Spaepen et al., 2007.

claim: Many members of the Roseobacter group have multiple metabolic pathways for IAA synthesis.
source: As many members of the Roseobacter group have multiple metabolic pathways for IAA synthesis (Moran et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moran et al., 2007.

claim: The hormetic effect of IAA has been previously described; IAA promotes plant growth at low concentration while acting as a growth inhibitor at high concentrations.
source: The hormetic effect of IAA has been previously described; IAA promotes plant growth at low concentration while acting as a growth inhibitor at high concentrations (Persello-Cartieaux et al., 2001, 2003; Xie et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Persello-Cartieaux et al., 2001, 2003; Xie et al., 1996.

claim: Similar hormetic effects of IAA were observed when increasing concentrations of IAA were added to a culture of diatoms.
source: Similar effects were observed when increasing concentrations of IAA were added to a culture of diatoms (Amin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Amin et al., 2015.

claim: In various bacteria, attempts to perturb IAA synthesis were unsuccessful due to multiple redundant biosynthetic pathways.
source: In various bacteria, attempts to perturb IAA synthesis were unsuccessful due to multiple redundant biosynthetic pathways (Spaepen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Spaepen et al., 2007.

claim: Tryptophan released by a diatom fuels IAA production by a bacterium.
source: In line with this idea, in another algal-bacterial interaction it has been shown that tryptophan released by a diatom fuels IAA production by a bacterium (Amin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Amin et al., 2015.

claim: Viral infection is key in E. huxleyi blooms' demise.
source: It is known that viral infection is key in the blooms' demise (Bratbak et al., 1993; Lehahn et al., 2014; Vardi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bratbak et al., 1993; Lehahn et al., 2014; Vardi et al., 2012.

claim: Environmental stresses such as nutrient depletion as well as viral infection have been shown to enhance PCD in E. huxleyi.
source: Environmental stresses such as nutrient depletion as well as viral infection have been shown to enhance PCD in E. huxleyi (Bidle, 2015, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bidle, 2015, 2016.

claim: Planktonic bacteria crowd around a lysing microalga, feeding off the released cellular content.
source: Recently, Smirga and colleagues demonstrated experimentally how planktonic bacteria crowd around a lysing microalga, feeding off the released cellular content (Smriga et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smriga et al., 2016.

claim: Microzooplankton display higher growth rates when feeding on naked E. huxleyi cells in comparison to calcified cells.
source: It has been previously demonstrated that microzooplankton display higher growth rates when feeding on naked E. huxleyi cells in comparison to calcified cells (Harvey et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harvey et al., 2015.

claim: Reversible modes of attachment were shown to take place when bacteria such as A. tumefaciens are assessing whether or not to attach to a substrate in a new environment.
source: Reversible modes of attachment were shown to take place when bacteria such as A. tumefaciens are assessing whether or not to attach to a substrate in a new environment (Heindl et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heindl et al., 2014.

claim: A. tumefaciens and P. inhibens both attach through their pole to their host.
source: Several similarities between A. tumefaciens and P. inhibens seem to exist; both attach through their pole to their host (Heindl et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heindl et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2013.

claim: Both A. tumefaciens and P. inhibens express a polar polysaccharide involved in bacterial attachment.
source: both express a polar polysaccharide involved in bacterial attachment (Heindl et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heindl et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2013.

claim: Both A. tumefaciens and P. inhibens utilize IAA to manipulate the growth of their host.
source: both utilize IAA to manipulate the growth of their host (Subramoni et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Subramoni et al., 2014.

claim: In A. tumefaciens, IAA is produced to enhance growth of plant tissue while creating tumors.
source: In the association of the plant pathogen Agrobacterium tumefaciens with its hosts, IAA is central too (Spaepen et al., 2007; Subramoni et al., 2014). It is produced to enhance growth of plant tissue while creating tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Spaepen et al., 2007; Subramoni et al., 2014.

claim: Roseobacters possess the ability to chemotax.
